0.title: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering
0.body: “But see, amid the mimic rout A crawling shape intrude! A blood-red thing that writhes from out The scenic solitude! It writhes! — it writhes! — with mortal pangs The mimes become its food, And seraphs sob at vermin fangs In human gore imbued. While the angels, all pallid and wan, Uprising, unveiling, affirm That the play is the tragedy, ‘Man,’ And its hero the Conqueror Worm.” – Ligeia, Edgar Allen Poe Dragons are a mystery. Dragons make dungeons full of magical traps. No one knows why. Dragons do not speak the common language, and attempts to communicate with them have driven sorcerers insane. They may not be evil, but they are so far away from humanity that you might as well call them such. Mesi, the ancient philosopher, theorized that dragons domesticate and cultivate humans in the same way humans cultivate cattle, and no modern discussion of dragons fails to bring up (and usually disagree with) this curious point. The fact is, nobody knows much about dragons. (Dragons steal princesses, too. No one is sure why, either.)

1.title: The GM’s Manifesto
1.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › The GM’s Manifesto
1.body: A game is all about decisions. That is essentially what every game is, whether it's a traditional game like poker, or a board game, or an RPG. A role-playing game’s play happens via discussion. The GM describes things, the players ask questions, the GM elaborates, the players describe things, the GM asks questions, the players elaborate, and the process repeats. It’s a back-and-forth—asking questions and answering them. During this exchange, the GM and the players make decisions. This is what’s fun about RPGs. Therefore, your job is to create interesting decisions for the players. Some advice to this end: - Create environments that incite interesting decisions - Create characters and factions with interesting motivations - Describe the environment fully, engaging sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch - Act in good faith by speaking generously - Referee player actions fairly

2.title: Create meaningful exploration
2.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › The GM’s Manifesto › Create meaningful exploration
2.body: Decisions in an RPG should be interesting, not arbitrary. It is essential that, during the Crawl, you provide meaningful choices so that exploration is both fun and engaging. An empty hallway with two branching paths doesn’t give the players enough information to make an informed or interesting choice. A coin flip could determine the “best” way to go. However, you could put Cant graffiti on the walls of the right path that reads: “Undead ahead! Do not enter! Turn back! All is lost!” If the players listen at the left path, they could hear the distinctively peacock-esque cry of the cockatrice. Now the players have information to make a decision: would they rather face a cockatrice or the undead? What are they most prepared for? Could they lure the undead towards the cockatrice? Broadcast dangers. Hide treasures behind clues that make players feel clever. Create meaningful choices so that your players can make informed decisions.

3.title: Create engaging personas
3.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › The GM’s Manifesto › Create engaging personas
3.body: The Underworld and the City should both be full of memorable characters with their own interesting motivations. Each of the GM’s characters has a personality defined by their likes, dislikes, wants, and needs. In the same way that dangers should be broadcast, so should your characters’ personalities. By clearly showing what a character’s likes and dislikes are, players will be given opportunities to role-play meaningfully. The Underworld is deadly enough that not every single denizen needs to be hostile. The Disposition rules (Social Encounters & Disposition) make sure that players have a fair shake when encountering new characters. Give players opportunities to gather information, make unlikely allies, and take part in factional intrigue.

4.title: Engage the senses
4.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › The GM’s Manifesto › Engage the senses
4.body: Meaningful exploration only works when the players have a good sense of what is going on. Players need you to tell them as much information as possible about the environment they are acting within. Paint pictures with your descriptions, actually sketch out rooms when mental pictures are difficult to conjure, and be vivid about all five senses. Don’t leave out any salient details about things that players can see, hear, feel, or smell.

5.title: Speak generously
5.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › The GM’s Manifesto › Speak generously
5.body: Don’t fall into the trap of thinking that half-secrets and hints are interesting. Information-sharing games are only fun when information is actually shared. Maybe the information comes with a price (“You’re not sure if the dragon is truly sleeping or only faking it. You’ll have to move closer to get a better look at him…”), but when it comes time to pay the piper, give the players as much information as you can. “Gotcha” moments are not fun. This is particularly true when players bid lore. If you accept a lore bid, you have a social obligation to speak generously to the player and give as much information as is appropriate.

6.title: Be a fair arbiter
6.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › The GM’s Manifesto › Be a fair arbiter
6.body: Arbitrating Rules Questions What should be done if there is a rules dispute during gameplay? One of the GM's duties is to settle these questions and decide how the rule should be played. If you're still learning the game, you might want to look them up every time until the flow of narrative and mechanics feels natural. If you have the rules down pretty well but encounter a speedbump, we offer this suggestion: decide in favor of the players and look up the rule later. Don't slow down a fun combat with page turning. Just make a temporary rule that is beneficial for the players and ask your best rules lawyer at the table to look it up after the combat is over. Let player decisions carry weight. If the players come up with ideas that should work, you don’t even need to touch the cards. Their plan can simply work. What makes sense comes before the rules. At the same time, don’t pull punches. Victories are only valuable if defeat is a real possibility. You are neither the players’ antagonist nor their friend. One of your roles is to be a neutral interpreter of the physics of the imaginary world. There are random elements. Interpret them judiciously. As much as possible, make the mechanics visible. Say what you’re doing, what the players are testing fate for, and what the results will be. As the GM, you can give difficult situations to the players with no idea how to solve them yourself. The players will surprise you with their ingenuity and problem-solving skills. When they come up with something surprising and cool that should work, let it work. “Deep in the human unconscious is a pervasive need for a logical universe that makes sense. But the real universe is always one step beyond logic.” – Dune, Frank Herbert

7.title: Running the Crawl Phase
7.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase
7.body: The standard flow of the Crawl is as follows: The players declare where they intend to go. If the guild begins this phase by leaving the City, they declare which entrance to the Underworld they will use. If the guild is in the Underworld, they declare the direction they move (e.g., “We’ll go towards room 12 to the east.”) - The GM draws a card from the major arcana for the Meatgrinder. - The GM asks, “What light do you have? Based on what the players can see, the GM describes the room’s contents in addition to the Meatgrinder results. The GM asks, “What do you do?” - The players ask the GM questions about the environment. - The players describe their actions. - To help adjudicate, the GM asks, “What do you have in your hands?” The GM arbitrates the results of the players’ actions. The GM calls for tests of fate when the situation is tense and failure is interesting. This entire process repeats.

8.title: Creating your Underworld
8.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › Creating your Underworld
8.body: Homebrewing Running a game is sort of like cooking. The first few times you do it, you adhere judiciously to a recipe. However, the more you cook, the more that repetition, experimentation, improvisation, and restriction reveals the methodology and chemistry that underlies the recipes. This game is a complete package but it is just a recipe. It has an underlying chemistry that produces a particular taste. The more you play it, the more you’ll understand how the parts and pieces work together. Once you do, you’ll understand how to change parts of it to better suit your tastes. The game is better when the book is not the authority; rather, authority is given to the GM and the general will of the table. If this book mentions something in passing like, say, lycanthropy, we haven’t felt the need to give you paragraphs and paragraphs of crunch on the subject. RPGs have been going on for a few decades now. There’s information out there. Find some time between sessions to create some lycanthropy rules that you like. Make the lore work for the game world that you’ve made. Get player buy-in about the idea and get everybody excited about it. You own the act of mapping the dungeon, inventing the stats for monsters, designing traps to be overcome, and hiding rewards. His Majesty the Worm front-loads this work. Before you start running a game, you’ll want to sit down and sketch out the entire Underworld megadungeon that you’ll be using. Appendix E deals with generating your Underworld megadungeon. Doing this work over the course of one or two Sunday afternoons frees you from doing weekly game session planning. You’ve done the hard work already. The City Phase will be your trigger to keep your dungeons fresh: this is when you think about how the players have changed the situation in the Underworld, update your notes accordingly, and create new Meatgrinder entries to replace the ones the players have already seen.

9.title: Creating a soundscape
9.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › Creating your Underworld › Creating a soundscape
9.body: You can provide a sense of consistency and theme for the different dungeons of your Underworld by building a bespoke playlist. Associate each level with a specific song. When the players enter a dungeon, play its theme song on a loop. (Choosing a music player with a looping option is important. Spotify works well.) You can also have theme music for the beginning and ending of a session, for Challenges, and for recurring GM characters. Video game music works well for this purpose. It’s designed to fade into the background and create an atmosphere. Be aware that your players may indelibly associate the music with that particular video game, taking them out of the His Majesty the Worm experience. Choose your favorite music from obscure games or games you know your table hasn’t played overmuch. Your mileage may vary. Some players find any music—even music without lyrics—to be very distracting. Ask your table what they prefer. “Wherefore each of you, when his turn comes, must go down to the general underground abode, and get the habit of seeing in the dark.” – “The Allegory of the Cave,” The Republic, Plato

10.title: Creating interesting characters
10.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › Creating interesting characters
10.body: It’s your job to portray characters with personalities that are evocative, strange, conflicting, and clearly broadcast. This is true for all creatures that you control, no matter how monstrous! Each character you introduce should have a personality defined by their dislikes and likes, wants and needs . - Dislikes are gates to the character’s heart. - Likes are the key. - Wants are aspirational character desires. - Needs are foundational character desires. Understanding a character’s personality allows you to arbitrate the guild’s attempts to bargain with them fairly. Reference the Dispositions see Social Encounters & Disposition for role-playing guidance.

11.title: Dislikes
11.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › Creating interesting characters › Dislikes
11.body: Dislikes trigger negative Dispositions like distaste or anger. - These triggers can be behaviors (“lying”) or traits (“all elves”). - GM characters won’t bargain with adventurers that they dislike.

12.title: Likes
12.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › Creating interesting characters › Likes
12.body: Likes trigger positive Dispositions like trust or joy. - These triggers can be behaviors (“sharing alcohol”) or traits (“good at music”). - GM characters will bargain fairly with adventurers that they like.

13.title: Wants
13.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › Creating interesting characters › Wants
13.body: Wants fulfill the character’s wishes. - Wants are discrete. They can be items (“enough money for a dowry”) or events (“marry the widow Prescott”). - If a GM character is offered something they want as a bargaining chip, tests of fate to manipulate them are made with favor.

14.title: Needs
14.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › Creating interesting characters › Needs
14.body: Needs represent the status quo. - Needs are abstract and essential (“for Baron Afanas to stay in power so the peasants continue to pay their taxes to me”). - If a GM character’s needs are threatened as a bargaining chip, tests of Wands to manipulate them are made with favor but their Disposition will be a hostile one, such as anger or distaste. They won’t bargain again. Contrasting or conflicting likes, dislikes, wants, and needs ensures that the players have multiple ways to interact with GM characters. For instance, some mermaids might like gossip and want to eat a man’s eyes, the tips of his fingers, and his privates . A guild of men encountering mermaids are likely targets to be devoured. However, if the guild feed the mermaids juicy gossip instead, they might avoid a combat encounter.

15.title: The blessing of chaos
15.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › The blessing of chaos
15.body: Sometimes Meatgrinder events target random adventurers. Sometimes you can imagine a few equally reasonable possibilities and want some help making a fair decision. You can use the cards as a random oracle to help you make choices. Expose this randomness to your table. It will make you seem more “fair.” You can alleviate some of the harshest feelings of injustice by leaving an adventurer’s fate up to the cards. Here are some tips for handling random events during the flow of gameplay.

16.title: Events targeting an adventurer
16.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › The blessing of chaos › Events targeting an adventurer
16.body: Sometimes, a Meatgrinder event targets one particular adventurer. This should make sense in context: the first person in the marching order might blunder into the trap, whereas the last one in marching order doesn’t notice that their potion bottle is broken and leaking. Sometimes, Meatgrinder events or an enemy’s attack targets a random adventurer. In this event, consult the top card of the minor arcana discard pile. The random effect will target the player whose path matches that suit. If you have multiple people with that path at the table, use the card’s value to choose between them in a quick way (e.g., odd is the first player to your left, even is the first player to your right).

17.title: Events targeting equipment
17.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › The blessing of chaos › Events targeting equipment
17.body: You’ll notice that the adventurer sheet has four belt slots and twenty-one pack slots. These numbers were intentionally chosen. If you need to target a player’s belt slot with a Meatgrinder event, glance at the minor arcana’s discard pile and note the top card’s suit for a random number 1–4. -

18.title: What are you holding?
18.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › What are you holding?
18.body: There is one question that helps inform your adjudication of all other player actions: “What do you have in your hands right now?” This is the most important question in your GM tool kit . Anything an adventurer attempts might be hampered or helped by the answer.

19.title: Example the first
19.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › What are you holding? › Example the first
19.body: Player: Can I climb the wall here and look over it? GM: Well, the wall is made of crumbling brick, so sure, it would be easy. What are you carrying? Player: I'll leave my sword and shield on the ground. GM: OK. So, you prop your sword and shield against the wall and start climbing the wall?

20.title: Example the second
20.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › What are you holding? › Example the second
20.body: Player: OK, I want to try and pick the lock on the weird door with the face. GM: Who has the light source? (A variation on “What's in your hands?”) Player 2: I do. I'm standing guard by the first room to make sure nobody ambushes us. GM: If you're trying to pick the lock but your light source is at the cavern's opening, you basically can't see what you're doing. That'll be disfavor for sure. Player 3: I'll pull out my torch and light it off of Player 2's and stand near the locked door to provide light. GM: OK, that works. Test fate with Pentacles. The fiction of what an adventurer is holding gives you immediate context for the rest of the scene.

21.title: How much treasure?
21.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › How much treasure?
21.body: You might ask “How much treasure should I give the players?” This is not the right way to think about it. Riches and life are both cheap, and can be quickly lost. Remember that the luxurious upkeep in the City is 100 gold. Getting this can feel like a major reward. If players land a major haul, having a few City Phases where they live in the lap of luxury will reinforce the feeling that they had a major accomplishment. After that money is gone, they will return to more humble living.

22.title: What can I see?
22.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › What can I see?
22.body: When a player asks what their adventurer can see, describe everything in the room that they could possibly see or notice. This gives players enough context to actually interact with the room in a meaningful way. This information is filtered by a few factors, of course. An adventurer might not be able to see in the dark, but they could still hear their environment. They won't be able to see hidden or obscured objects (like a secret door or a thief hiding behind a curtain), but are free to search in more thorough ways. Essentially, there are three levels of information based on how thoroughly an adventurer looks around them. No tests are required and no cards need to be drawn; the only thing that is tested is a player’s thoughtfulness while asking questions. 1. Glancing: This covers everything that can be perceived in an area by someone who has good light. 2. Scrutinizing: Gated, until the players ask questions. “Is the gargoyle made of stone?” “What color is the book?” “What are the pages made out of?” “Are the hinges inside or out?” 3. Investigatory: Gated, until the adventurers interact with the environment. “I try to twist the moose head. Does it feel like it has any give?” “ I’ll pull back the tapestry. Is there anything behind it?” “I tap on the walls. Do they sound hollow?” Information should only rarely be held back from the players. Be charitable in the information you give: the more information a player has, the more interesting choices they can make. So, even in a room with a secret door, the adventurer might feel a slight draft in the room that reveals that something is amiss. Or if there was a thief behind a curtain, they might hear a muffled cough for a moment, but then nothing.

23.title: What do I know?
23.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Crawl Phase › What do I know?
23.body: When a player asks, “Would my character know about X?” make a quick call on how obscure the question is. If the question is something their adventurer might possibly know, speak generously about the subject. If the question is obscure, ask the player if they have a motif they could use to bid lore. There are essentially two levels of knowledge. 1. Obvious knowledge: This covers stuff everybody knows and sets the general expectations of a situation. Giving players a lot of information makes sure that both players and the GM are on the same page and lets players make intelligent choices. 2. Obscure knowledge: Some specialist subjects are only going to be known to certain people. Obscure knowledge might include the habits of supernatural creatures, the likes and dislikes of specific people within an organization, or the metaphysics of the planes of reality. This information should only be given to players who bid lore . If a player bids lore and you accept the question, give as much information on the subject as you know—just keep talking and riffing until you run out of material.

24.title: Running the Challenge Phase
24.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase
24.body: The Challenge rules resolve questions of timing between hostile forces in a fair and fun way. Actions like “We all run past the imps and slam the door” and “I want to shoot an arrow at the lich before they complete the ritual” are best answered by using the timing of the Challenge Phase. The Crawl Phase can transition to the Challenge Phase and back organically. When there’s tension and a hostile situation does not seem resolvable with a single test of fate, call for a Challenge Phase. When the opposition is defeated, the outcome of the Challenge is clear, or the players want to retreat, transition back into the Crawl.

25.title: Creating interesting locations
25.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting locations
25.body: When possible, Challenges should take place somewhere cool . Cool encounter spaces provide potential energy—they give the players (and the GM!) stuff to interact with. Scatter one or two interactable pieces of scenery across each zone, including dynamic terrain , sensory information , and usable objects .

26.title: Terrain
26.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting locations › Terrain
26.body: Create spaces that tell a story. Challenges often inhabit a liminal space, set between safety and danger, stable and unstable, solid and liquid, cool and hot, heights and depths. Exploit these contrasts.

27.title: Sensory information
27.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting locations › Sensory information
27.body: An adventurer’s understanding of their environment is based on the limits of their senses. By default, the Underworld is a dark and difficult place. Place further restrictions on the guild’s vision, hearing, and other senses to provide additional challenges.

28.title: Objects
28.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting locations › Objects
28.body: Empty rooms are boring. Each space should be scattered with interesting items. Set pieces can be picked up, hidden behind, or smashed through. Terrain Sensory information Objects --- --- --- A bridge over a chasm Smoke near the room’s ceiling, choking or blinding tall characters Hanging tapestries A 45° collapsed obelisk Fungus that extrudes choking spores, lights, or sounds when bumped into Braziers of coals Chains hanging from the ceiling Fog near the room’s floor, obscuring short characters Silk dressing screens Icy floors A colossal ringing bell, deafening all nearby Tables and chairs A climbable idol Blinding light emanating from a bright red ruby Bookshelves Hanging chandeliers The area is half-filled with murky water Taxidermied monsters Quaking floors Illusory objects and creatures Fountains An oil slick Shrieking wind, preventing flight or missile weapons Weapon racks

29.title: Creating interesting battles
29.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting battles
29.body: Your job as the GM is to keep the Challenge flowing. You track the Initiative count, lead discussions about rules, and make rule calls when players attempt different types of actions. And, importantly, you control the antagonists during the Challenge. Here are some lessons learned during playtesting to help you create tactically difficult and rewarding Challenges.

30.title: Gang up on the players
30.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting battles › Gang up on the players
30.body: Players have more cards in total than the GM. They will act more often. However, you have an advantage when it comes to the number of antagonists. - With multiple enemies, each action you use can target the same number of adventurers. If five goblins use the Attack action, this will affect up to five different adventurers. - Enemies can also focus fire, attacking the same adventurer. Use the rules for mobs see Play Initiative for each significant enemy to good effect. - The GM’s “side” can often absorb more Wounds than the players. The gimmick is that players feel cool as they mow down hordes of zombies or bandits or whatever. At the same time, it’s a war of attrition—the GM can put pressure on the players as they face hordes of enemies.

31.title: Make minor actions as often as possible
31.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting battles › Make minor actions as often as possible
31.body: You have much more freedom than players when it comes to card choice because you don’t have to worry about card suits. As such, take minor actions as often as possible. Smart players will try to keep the monsters “stun-locked” with Roughhouse and various effects. Smart GMs will use Recover, which doesn’t have a requisite value—simply discard any lesser doom card as a minor action to keep your antagonists free and ready to act.

32.title: Fight dirty, fight fair
32.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting battles › Fight dirty, fight fair
32.body: Don’t pull punches, but fight fair. Don’t change your monsters’ stats halfway through a battle. If the players come up with an amazing plan and shove your big bad guy off of a tower, let it happen. Of course, what is good for the goose is good for the gander. If the players start shoving your Balrog off the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, you can pull their wizard off of it just as easily (if you have the appropriate card). If the players are losing, they have a choice to make: stand and fight, run away, or talk their way out of it. The Disposition and Morale rules make sure that the players have ample opportunities to talk their way out of a fight at pretty much any stage.

33.title: Creating interesting antagonists
33.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating interesting antagonists
33.body: Challenges that just consist of “smack the other guy dead” can be boring. Make fights with goals other than defeating the enemy. To this end, create antagonists with potential energy . For example, if a Meatgrinder encounter simply lists “1–4 skeletons,” the Challenge Phase will consist of the antagonists whacking each other until one side expires from Wounds. However, if the Meatgrinder details, “1–4 skeletons in a pit that seem to be guarding a skeleton with a golden crown; the crowned skeleton is not moving,” the encounter gains more texture and raises several questions: - Can the adventurers get the crown off of the king skeleton safely? - What happens if they do? Does this trigger something? - What is the story of these undead? How does it relate to this region of the Underworld? - How can the pit be safely navigated by the adventurers? As the guild moves through the Underworld, the potential energy from one antagonist will transfer onto another until eventually there is an explosion—with the players caught in the middle.

34.title: Creating surprises
34.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Challenge Phase › Creating surprises
34.body: If things are beginning to get stagnant, introduce something that changes the Challenge dramatically. Let the potential energy transfer into kinetic energy . Here’s a table to inspire ideas for different ways to shake things up. Glance at the top of the minor arcana discard pile for a random event: Card Twist :---: --- I The current conflict smashes down a nearby wall, connecting the current room to an adjacent one. What dwells in that room, and how will it interact with the current scene? II A wandering monster wanders into the scene. III An infantile wandering monster wanders into the scene. It imprints onto a random adventurer. IV A rival adventuring party, currently struggling with problems of their own, crash onto the scene. V Something in the current scene is revealed to only be an illusion. VI Something in the scene is revealed, with further investigation, to be something completely different. The orc is just three goblins in a trench coat. The gargoyle is just a statue. VII A secret passage is revealed, leading to hidden treasure or danger. VIII A chance blow rips open a backpack, causing two alchemical potions to crash onto the ground. As the two reagents mix, a terrible ooze begins to form, farting out magical clouds as it does. IX Disembodied spirits climb inside the bodies of nearby slain foes and reanimate them as flesh puppets. The spirits have their own agendas. What do they want? X A dropped torch or knocked over brazier starts a fire which quickly becomes a hazard as the area is filled with smoke and flames. Page The area becomes suddenly flooded with water/wine/sludge/something else. What is the source of this deluge? Knight The next time an adventurer is dealt a Wound, they are dazed. When they come to their senses, they distinctly remember a preternatural voice speaking to them. What is this divine revelation? Is it real? Or is there something going wrong in the unknowable space behind their eyes that’s undiagnosed? Queen Death shows up and stands quietly in the corner. He’s a few minutes early, but is willing to wait. King A stampede of doppelgangers barrels down the passage and accidentally bumps into the guild. They get all tangled up, tripping over each other. After the confusion, the party is substantially larger. Each player has at least two, but maybe as many as four new adventurers. Not even the players are sure who is who. Give them new adventurer sheets for their clones until things are sorted out.

35.title: Running the Camp Phase
35.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Camp Phase
35.body: Camping scenes are moments of relative calm within the frenetic journey of the Underworld. They are explicitly times for a guild to regroup, role-play with each other, and recover near the warm light of the campfire before moving on into the waiting darkness; a time for the whole table to breathe a sigh of relief. The GM’s job is two-fold during the Camp Phase: - Act as the master of ceremonies to make sure that the Camp Phase flows smoothly, adjudicating any rules questions that come up - Inject color into the scenes of the encampment The latter is done by asking questions. For the vast majority of the game, you have to be “on”: you describe the setting, interpret the Meatgrinder results, role-play various characters. The Camp Phase is an opportunity for you to take a break, too. Give some of the narrative work to players: ask them to describe their gear, how they set up camp, what sort of rations they’re preparing, etc. When the adventurers break bread (step 2), you can provide some discussion prompts and ask for a small scene to be role-played out. Frame these questions as subjects the entire guild is discussing: for example, “You’re all discussing the worst injuries you’ve had. What are your scars and where did you get them?” Whenever the players riff on these questions, they provide you free ideas. Take notes about what the players are talking about at camp. Use them to seed the content of the City Phase! - Did a player riff a story about their childhood sweetheart? Create a special City event where she invites them to her wedding. Will they accept? - Did a player mention their mother’s famous lemon tart? When they get back to the City, she’s mailed them one—a free ration for the next crawl! - Did a player mention an old enemy? Place their enemy in the City. Next time they surface, she approaches them on the street and asks to bury the hatchet. How will they react? Don’t fall into the trap of thinking that punishment equals good role-playing. Don’t go and kill old loves, parents, friends. Rather, draw these personas into the story and create flash points for the players to act.

36.title: 50 campfire discussions
36.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the Camp Phase › 50 campfire discussions
36.body: 1. What’s special about your weapon? 2. What do you currently look like? Has adventuring torn or tarnished your once-pristine gear? 3. What’s your favorite personal possession? 4. What weird traits does your animal companion have? 5. Who were your parents? Are they alive? 6. What songs do they sing in your homeland? 7. What was your first adventure into the Underworld? 8. Would you rather eat a plate of maggots, or have a hundred maggots placed secretly in your food over the course of a year? 9. Do you have any tattoos? Why did you choose them? 10. Who was your first kiss? 11. When did you lose your virginity? 12. When was the first time you saw magic performed? 13. If you could learn another language, what would it be? 14. What monster was the scariest for you to fight? Why? 15. When did you learn how to swim? 16. What’s your favorite food? 17. What’s something you’re afraid to lose? 18. What do you miss about your homeland? 19. Kill/marry/fuck your other guild members? 20. What was your first pet? What was his name? 21. What was the worst quest you ever had? 22. What was your first job? 23. Would you rather give up cheese or oral sex? 24. What’s your home life? Do you have a partner? Children? 25. When was the last time you cried? Why? 26. What’s your favorite game? 27. Would you rather be famous while you’re alive and forgotten afterwards, or unknown during life and revered after death? 28. What’s one item at the top of your bucket list? 29. What’s your favorite alcoholic drink? Is there one you refuse to drink? 30. What is your greatest achievement? 31. What was the last dream you had? 32. Would you rather fight twelve child zombies or one zombie troll? 33. If a sorcerer transformed you into an animal, but you had a choice, what animal would you choose to become? 34. Is there any quest you would flatly refuse to do? 35. What’s the dumbest thing you’ve ever done? 36. What do you have in your pockets? 37. What would you do with 1,000g in your pocket right now? 38. What’s something you love about another guild member? 39. How many three-year-olds could you fight at once? 40. Do you have any scars? Where did you get them? 41. Would you rather be a vampire or a werewolf? 42. What’s your favorite joke? 43. What’s something you’re looking forward to? 44. What’s something you want? 45. What’s a secret that you know? 46. What’s the last thing you masturbated to? 47. When’s the first time you took a life? 48. What’s something you’d change about yourself? 49. Just how old are you anyway? When’s your birthday? 50. What is best in life?

37.title: Running the City Phase
37.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the City Phase
37.body: Social encounters in the City aren’t like social encounters in the Underworld. In the Underworld, the characters are invaders. In the City, characters are part of the ecosystem. That is a fundamentally different paradigm. Through role-playing, the City blooms for the players. However, the players must find the appropriate keys for the gates that are placed in front of them. The GM’s job is threefold: Find what goals the players have, clearly define what is needed to achieve those goals, and create interesting obstacles.

38.title: Seed and grow goals
38.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the City Phase › Seed and grow goals
38.body: In the earliest sessions of the game, a player might have no specific goals or desires in the City. That’s fine. However, as a GM, it’s your job to lure them into the web of intrigue that makes the City Phase especially interesting. This is done by clearly showing the resources, boons, and wish fulfillment that can be gained by interacting with the City factions. Initially, players may be interested in simple things: more money and more power. Again—that’s fine. Use these incentives as lures to a world of actual intrigue. As players get embroiled in factional strife, different goals will begin to emerge from base needs. As with the Underworld, the City should be bizarre and complex. The City creation rules in Appendix D are designed to be evocative and inspiring. The setting is an anti-canon. Throw out ideas that don’t work for your game. Jam other shit in there. The people in the City should be evocative, scary, funny, weird, and interesting. The organizations should feel both rooted in history and fantastic. As a hint, nothing you can come up with will be weirder than history already is. Read a lot, collect a lot of ideas, and mash them together into your City. Broadcast all the districts and special City Actions available to your players. Create a shared document detailing all the things players can do in the City . This lets players make informed decisions. Players will be obliged to take studious notes, draw relationship maps, track favors owed, keep journals about the various likes and dislikes of various GM characters, etc. Figuring out how to navigate the social situations of the City Phase replicates the fun of discovery found during the Crawl Phase.

39.title: Create a path to success
39.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the City Phase › Create a path to success
39.body: Don’t be coy about how players might achieve their goals. It’s not actually fun to be mysterious: it engenders a sense of mistrust between the GM and the players. If a player can declare a clear goal, you can provide a clear path towards that goal. The Support City Action is the main tool that players have to make meaningful progress towards open-ended goals . Create a consistent metric for how you set complexity when adventurers are performing the Support action. Be open-minded when players propose actions that tick off complexity.

40.title: Example
40.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the City Phase › Create a path to success › Example
40.body: Player: I want to become the most respected mead maker in the City. GM: OK. First, you have to actually build your meadery. That’s a Building action. “Meadery” is three syllables, so it’s going to take at least 150g to open your most basic, hole-in-the-wall joint. The fancier you want it to be, you can add more description for more money. Player: I want it, literally, to be the “best meadery in the City.” That’s… eight syllables. So 400g. GM: I agree. Then, you have to woo and court influential members of the aristocracy to hype your meadery. Starting complexity for basic tasks is at least complexity 3, but because being the best anything in the City is difficult, let’s set the Support action to 5 complexity.

41.title: Create obstacles
41.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the City Phase › Create obstacles
41.body: At the same time, you should make the paths to success fraught with peril. As the adventurers rise in the City, they’ll undoubtedly brush shoulders with powers that do not want any rivals. These rivals can put roadblocks in their way. These dangers should not be easily perceived. Surprise setbacks are fair game; they test the players’ creativity and ability to react to new information. Do not unmake a player’s progress. If the GM burns down the meadery from the previous example, the player probably has good reason to be grumpy. Rather, introduce roadblocks. For example, perhaps a rival bribes the tradesman’s union so that they will no longer do work for an adventurer—to use the Build action, the adventurer must get the union back on their side. Importantly, the City is a place of laws. Murdering everything in the Underworld may be a strategy that gets results, but in the City it gets you jailed and executed. The players cannot kill their way out of social situations. In general, we recommend not using the Challenge Phase rules at all in the City. If the players are contemplating some violence, reduce it to a Swords test. On a success, the players have won and can declare what sort of punishment they deal out: do they kill their opponent or simply slap them around a little? Depending on what damage is dealt and the relative social status of those involved, you can decide on the “appropriate” response from the All-Watch—the response from those in power is never commensurate.

42.title: Completing quests and soft endings
42.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Running the City Phase › Completing quests and soft endings
42.body: The nature of the sandbox can make it tricky to know when the game is “over.” A more plot-driven game might be over when the players win or lose—the ring is cast into the fire, the Death Star is destroyed, everybody lives happily ever after. Not so in His Majesty the Worm. The players create their own quests and drive their own goals. When one adventurer’s quest is over, the rest of the guild still have quests to pursue. An adventurer’s career ends in two ways: death or retirement. It should be the goal of every player to finish their adventurer’s quest and retire to safety in the City. When one adventurer succeeds in their quest, it’s a good time to check in with your table. - Do the players want to keep playing? Whose quest should they pursue next? - Do the players want to continue playing His Majesty the Worm but in a new setting? Should you all remake the City and Underworld (see Appendices D and E) and make a new guild? - Does another player want to try their hand at GMing? - Does the table want to play something else for a while? There’re tons of cool games out there. You can keep playing His Majesty the Worm or take a break. Just check in and make sure everybody is having as much fun as possible. The game might never be “over”—you can come back to the game again and again, creating a long and fondly-remembered history.

43.title: Converting Other Games
43.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Converting Other Games
43.body: An advantage of OSR games is that it’s simple to convert between them. His Majesty the Worm plays like an oldschool game but is not a retroclone. A little braingrease must be applied to convert rules, modules, and monsters into this game format, although it’s more of an art than a skill. Here are some guidelines.

44.title: Player character stats
44.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Converting Other Games › Player character stats
44.body: Adventurers’ attribute ratings in His Majesty the Worm are roughly equivalent to attribute bonuses in retroclone systems. For example, “Strength - 17 (+3)” would be “Swords 3.”

45.title: OSR
45.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Converting Other Games › OSR
45.body: OSR His Majesty the Worm --- --- Strength bonus Swords score Dexterity bonus Pentacles score Wisdom bonus Cups score Charisma bonus Wands score Fighter Path of Swords Thief Path of Pentacles Cleric Path of Cups Magic-user Path of Wands Saving throws Tests of fate

46.title: Monster stats
46.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Converting Other Games › Monster stats
46.body: A retroclone monster’s Hit Dice (HD) = their Health and Defense . Monsters in His Majesty the Worm are about as tough as in a retroclone. Allocate the monster’s HD into a combination of Health or Defense. If a monster is very well armored (like a dragon), the Defense score will be higher. If a monster is very fast and hard to hit, the Health score will be higher. If you’re not sure, just make the monster’s Health and Defense roughly equivalent. For example, a 7HD dragon might have 2 Health, 5 Defense.

47.title: Combat
47.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Converting Other Games › Combat
47.body: “To-hit” and “damage” are mostly meaningless in His Majesty the Worm. A Wound is the average damage done by a single sword swing. If a monster does an overwhelming amount of damage, you can represent that in different ways. A giant’s hammer might deal 2 Wounds, whereas a dragon’s unblockable fire breath might deal a Piercing Wound.

48.title: Magic
48.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Converting Other Games › Magic
48.body: When converting spells, first look for an equivalent spell in Appendix A. Feather Fall can be represented by the Feather spell, Cause Wounds can be represented by Withering, and so on. Spells beyond the 2nd level might be beyond the scope of adventurer abilities in this game. If they are a core part of a monster’s move set, look at the Effects list and make a judgment about how best to represent that power here. “How they will rejoice in passing from darkness to light! How worthless to them will seem the honours and glories of the den! But now imagine further, that they descend into their old habitations—in that underground dwelling they will not see as well as their fellows, and will not be able to compete with them in the measurement of the shadows on the wall; there will be many jokes about the man who went on a visit to the sun and lost his eyes, and if they find anybody trying to set free and enlighten one of their number, they will put him to death, if they can catch him.” – “The Allegory of the Cave,” The Republic, Plato

49.title: Inspirational and Educational Reading
49.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading
49.body: Here are some things that we think are awesome. His Majesty the Worm wouldn’t exist without them. If you consume this media, you’ll get what we’re going for with this game.

50.title: Core inspiration
50.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Core inspiration
50.body: The central influences on His Majesty the Worm all happen to be comics. Not sure why comics were the main inspiration here; something about the visual medium and the vaguely alternate aesthetic? We don't know!

51.title: Dungeon Meshi by Ryoko Kui
51.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Core inspiration › Dungeon Meshi by Ryoko Kui
51.body: Dungeon Meshi is the most thoughtful treatment of the physicality of dungeoneering that we've ever read. The characters, their gear, and their journeys have a practical weight. Its considerations of exploration, food, and exhaustion are fun and evocative. This should be required reading for anybody that wants to ignore mundane gear or avoid tracking rations. You can run His Majesty the Worm as a Dungeon Meshi RPG if you swap the word “alchemy” for “cooking.”

52.title: House of Orr by Nolan T. Jones, Rilley Dutton, and Richard Zayas and artist Victoria Grace Elliott
52.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Core inspiration › House of Orr by Nolan T. Jones, Rilley Dutton, and Richard Zayas and artist Victoria Grace Elliott
52.body: A defunct and unfinished webcomic that is currently super hard to find on the internet. As such, apologies for including it here. That said, House of Orr genuinely shaped our thinking about “the party as a character.” In the setting, political capital is held by adventuring guilds. A struggling guild, the titular House of Orr (who, by tradition, requires all members to take on a new name with the element “Orr”—Orrlock, Orrdalf, Orrwyn, etc.), hopes to establish itself as a political power. With its whimsical elements, House of Orr is genuinely delightful. It evokes the sense of playfulness that we want a game of His Majesty the Worm to have.

53.title: I Roved Out In Search of Truth and Love by Alexis Flowers
53.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Core inspiration › I Roved Out In Search of Truth and Love by Alexis Flowers
53.body: A “warmly pornographic” comic. If you strip out all the pornography, you have a super fun fantasy story. If you strip out all the fantasy story, you have some damn good smut. It is humorous and beautiful in a way that we want a game of His Majesty the Worm to be. By default, His Majesty the Worm isn't pornographic—that would require a lot of buy-in, consent tools, etc. It's not the sort of game we’re trying to run 99% of the time. It is, however, an “adult” game. Adventurers can buy into relationships with each other by electing the Lovers Bond.

54.title: Rat Queens by Kurtis J. Wiebe and Roc Upchurch
54.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Core inspiration › Rat Queens by Kurtis J. Wiebe and Roc Upchurch
54.body: Goddamn, Rat Queens rules. The friendship and interactions between the Rat Queens illustrates the inter-party relationships of His Majesty the Worm. We want every adventure to delve into each character’s motivations, backstory, and friendships in the same way that Rat Queens does. The one-two punches (e.g., the Betty Climber) that the Rat Queens perform in combat are half the reason the Challenge system works the way it does, too. Aid each other in combat to get the BIG numbers.

55.title: Movies
55.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Movies

56.title: As Above, So Below
56.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Movies › As Above, So Below
56.body: A found footage film where archaeologists-cum-urban-explorers delve into the Paris catacombs. They find Templar tombs, treasure, out-of-place artifacts, demons, and doom. It’s a great example of having a mythic underworld sitting under a major metropolitan area.

57.title: Cube
57.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Movies › Cube
57.body: A group of people wake up in a bizarre complex of interconnected cubes that are also death traps. Slowly, they start to piece together the puzzle of how to navigate them safely. A great example of how claustrophobic and terrifying crawling through a deathtrap dungeon would be.

58.title: Indiana Jones
58.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Movies › Indiana Jones
58.body: The pulp content of the Indiana Jones movies makes them genre staples in terms of dungeon-crawling. Think about the cool traps in Raiders of the Lost Ark or the puzzles in The Last Crusade. It’s rare to see such careful attention to dungeon-crawling deliberately called out in popular media.

59.title: Labyrinth
59.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Movies › Labyrinth
59.body: A young woman’s baby brother is trapped in the center of a sprawling maze by the Goblin King and she has until midnight to rescue him. As she adventures through the maze, she solves riddles, makes allies, and overcomes challenges. Dungeon-crawling at its most delightful.

60.title: Spine of Night
60.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Movies › Spine of Night
60.body: Although it’s not about dungeon crawling, the sheer inventiveness of its ultra-gory, heavy-metal aesthetic is hard to rival. It deals with brutal warriors, greedy scholars, winged assassins, and power-mad sorcerers delving into powers that mortals were not meant to know. Watch it and be inspired.

61.title: Books
61.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Books

62.title: House of Leaves by Mark Z. Danielewski
62.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Books › House of Leaves by Mark Z. Danielewski
62.body: Several narratives beautifully woven together: an academic critique of a found footage horror film, the personal journal of a man’s descent into schizophrenia, letters from a character’s mother. House of Leaves plays with text in a way that few novels do. People say it’s weird but it’s honestly pretty gettable if you’re willing to give it a try.

63.title: Invisible Cities by Italo Calvino
63.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Books › Invisible Cities by Italo Calvino
63.body: Framed as a conversation between Marco Polo and Kublai Khan, Invisible Cities lists fifty-five fictitious cities and their fictitious histories. As a meditation on memory, it is excellent, compelling the reader to search for hidden meanings in the text. It is an example of what is meant by the term “ anti-canon .”

64.title: Piranesi by Susanna Clarke
64.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Books › Piranesi by Susanna Clarke
64.body: The titular character lives (almost) alone in a museum world comprising three floors: a flooded basement, sprawling central corridors, and the occasional bird winging through the upper stories. An excellent example of what a mythic Underworld might feel like.

65.title: Tombs of Atuan by Ursula K. LeGuin
65.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Books › Tombs of Atuan by Ursula K. LeGuin
65.body: In this novel, the main character is a priestess of the Old Powers. She tends a lightless labyrinth of tombs—a labyrinth with a dark, unknown purpose. Forty-percent of the story is told without the visual sense; this seems like an impossible task but is wildly successful. Ultimately, this novel is one of the finest examples of fantasy fiction in the English language.

66.title: Blogs
66.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs
66.body: His Majesty the Worm suckled on the terrible, sweet milk that came out of the blogosphere during the nascence of the OSR movement. All posts listed below are online as of this printing.

67.title: “Blorb Principles,” from Idiomdrottning by Sandra Snan
67.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “Blorb Principles,” from Idiomdrottning by Sandra Snan
67.body: “Blorb” is a funny name given to a prep style that emphasizes preparing the game space thoroughly before players begin to interact with it. It advocates creating a robust setting up front so that the GM has to do very little (if any) improv during the game. In order of precedence, blorb prioritizes: 1. Prep 2. Procedure 3. Ideas that fill in the gaps between prep and procedure If this appeals to you, you will find a game type analogous to how His Majesty the Worm was played during its seven years of playtesting. Link: https://idiomdrottning.org/blorb-principles

68.title: “Dungeon Checklist,” from Goblinpunch by Arnold K
68.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “Dungeon Checklist,” from Goblinpunch by Arnold K
68.body: This is an excellent tool to use while building dungeons, and served as an inspiration for our own checklist in Appendix E. Link: http://goblinpunch.blogspot.com/2016/01/ dungeon-checklist.html

69.title: “The Dungeon as Mythic Underworld,” from Philotomy’s Musings by Jason Cone
69.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “The Dungeon as Mythic Underworld,” from Philotomy’s Musings by Jason Cone
69.body: Philotomy’s Musings is a collection of interpretive essays about OD&D that contained a revolutionary way to re-imagine megadungeons. The way it frames a dungeon as an inherently mythic space served as an inspiration for the core setting of this game. Link: https://save.vs.totalpartykill.ca/grab-bag/ philotomy/ (rehosted with permission)

70.title: “Handling IC Nastiness,” from Cavegirl’s Game Stuff by Emily Allen
70.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “Handling IC Nastiness,” from Cavegirl’s Game Stuff by Emily Allen
70.body: An essay on handling out-of-character traumas and phobias in an honest, collaborative way without using tools that might make players feel put in a spot. Link: http://cavegirlgames.blogspot.com/2019/02/ handling-ic-nastiness.html

71.title: “The ICI Doctrine: Information, Choice, Impact,” from Bastionland by Chris McDowall
71.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “The ICI Doctrine: Information, Choice, Impact,” from Bastionland by Chris McDowall
71.body: This essay articulates that creating a true sense of player agency is done by emphasizing information, choice, and impact. This is a fundamental text to understand how to best organize the conversation of role-playing games from a GM’s perspective. Link: https://www.bastionland.com/2018/09/the-icidoctrine-information-choice.html

72.title: “Landmark, Hidden, Secret” from DIY & Dragons by Anne
72.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “Landmark, Hidden, Secret” from DIY & Dragons by Anne
72.body: Inspiration for the way that His Majesty the Worm doles out information is drawn directly from this blog post. The post places all information on a continuum, from landmark (obvious) to hidden (requires cursory investigation) to secret (difficult to find). Link: https://diyanddragons.blogspot.com/2019/10/ landmark-hidden-secret.html

73.title: “In Corpathium,” from Last Gasp Grimoire by Logan Knight
73.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “In Corpathium,” from Last Gasp Grimoire by Logan Knight
73.body: The DNA of the City-creation rules in Appendix D are drawn from Logan Knight’s “Corpathium” setting. Link: https://www.lastgaspgrimoire.com/in-corpathium/

74.title: “Same Page Tool,” from Deeper in the Game by Christopher Chinn
74.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “Same Page Tool,” from Deeper in the Game by Christopher Chinn
74.body: The Same Page Tool is a great resource to help players and GMs understand what they want to get out of the game. It will be an asset while running session 0 and bringing new players into the game. Link: https://bankuei.wordpress.com/2010/03/27/the-same-page-tool/

75.title: “TFP DMG: How I Use Skills,” from Polemic, 10’ by James Young
75.breadcrumb: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering › Inspirational and Educational Reading › Blogs › “TFP DMG: How I Use Skills,” from Polemic, 10’ by James Young
75.body: A treatise on how to adjudicate tests of fate. The post argues that adventurers are competent and their skills (or motifs, in this game’s paradigm) should let them do crazy things. Call for tests of fate only when the adventurers are trying to go above and beyond. Link: http://tenfootpolemic.blogspot.com/2017/01/dmshit-how-i-use-skills.html

76.title: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens
76.body: Unleash the fury of your wrath, look at all who are proud and bring them low, look at all who are proud and humble them, crush the wicked where they stand. Bury them all in the dust together; shroud their faces in the grave. Job 40:11–13 In the early days, humans lived long, but were still subject to the laws of mortality. The First Death was a shock to everyone. It was hubris that made the Three Sisters try to steal the Well of Souls, also called the Underworld…hubris, as well as kindness. They thought that the power of the Well might make the dead live again. They thought the power of the Well might allow the sick and injured to receive healing. But it also brought the Worm. The Worm—the Oldest, the First of All Things, the Blind Maker—was the keeper of the Well of Souls. He was displeased by the Sister’s overreach. Long was the battle with the Worm. The Three Sisters sought to plunge Him deep into the earth, to banish Him back to His world. Though bound by their spells, He dragged them—and the Well—with Him. The First Empire of Man sank down beneath the earth, banished by their own power. Yet, He ever clawed upwards…and has now returned.

77.title: Monstrous Mixology
77.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology
77.body: The Cocktail Codex makes the bold claim that there are only six cocktails, with all cocktails being a variation of one of the core recipes. For example, vodka mixed with orange juice is a screwdriver. A variation on this recipe is a Cape Cod—vodka mixed with cranberry juice. Similarly, the game designer Chris McDowall makes the bold claim that the same can be true of RPG creatures. Every creature in a big monster manual is just a variation of one of the core mechanical recipes: an ogre is a strong and stupid humanoid monster; a zombie is a weak and stupid humanoid monster. Despite their differences, you can think of ogres and zombies as variations on a recipe.

78.title: Ingredients
78.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Ingredients
78.body: The two ingredients you mix together to make new creatures are theme and threat. There are templates provided for both. The combination of these templates will give you a starting place for the creature’s basic stats.

79.title: Theme
79.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Ingredients › Theme
79.body: Theme defines the creature’s mythological context. How is it fantastic? Creatures are grouped into six different themes: - Beast - Sorcerous - Elemental - Spirit - Man - Undead A creature’s theme defines some of their basic stats and lesser dooms.

80.title: Threat
80.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Ingredients › Threat
80.body: Threat defines the creature’s personality, tactics, and overall strength. How does it act? Creatures are grouped into five different levels of threat: - Minion - Elite - Brute - Dungeon Lord - Strategist A creature’s threat defines their attributes, their Health and Defense, and greater dooms. Importantly, creatures with the elite or dungeon lord threat templates prompt the GM to draw extra Challenge cards to represent their advanced powers; see Draw Challenge cards for full details.

81.title: Shaking up a new creature
81.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Shaking up a new creature
81.body: To create an interesting creature, start with a classic mythological monster. Define this creature by choosing both a theme and a threat. Then, exaggerate one aspect. People can only handle one new idea at a time, and changing too many things makes the creature lose its coherency. The exaggerated aspect will make the creature feel fresh and reinvigorate the player’s interest even in the most classic and overused monsters. Examples: - A zombie, but it's animated by a swarm of locusts - A giant spider, but its legs are human fingers - A skeleton, but it's covered in blood and in love with the skeleton inside of you Invent one or two dooms based on the exaggerated aspect. Examples of dooms can be found in the theme and threat templates. You can change any detail provided by a template to better fit your concept. Use this method to create creatures that are both gameable and gettable, familiar and fresh for your players. A Bestiary of pre-made denizens is provided in this appendix for your edification and expediency, starting see Bestiary. Use them to fill your dungeons. Change them to suit your purposes and predilections.

82.title: Creature Stats
82.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature Stats
82.body: A creature is defined by a small collection of stats that make it easy for the GM to interpret their abilities during play. Here’s a sample stat block of the skeleton below with some explanatory text. As a reminder, capitalized words in a dungeon denizen’s stats refer to effects. The rules for effects are listed in chapter 1.

83.title: Skeleton
83.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature Stats › Skeleton
83.body: Undead Brute When an undead has survived long enough for its flesh to rot, for its brains to be eaten by maggots, and for its eyes to jelly and fall out, it becomes a skeleton. Their existence is a curious perversion. How do they gambol about? How are their bones held together? What motivates them? The answer is hate. Skeletons hate the living. Living souls burn like torches in the blackness of the Underworld, and skeletons mindlessly seek to extinguish those bright lights. Skeletons sometimes pick up old and rusted weapons to channel their hate, but will also just plunge their bony fingers into an adventurer’s eye sockets. Sometimes, they wear rusted old armor. If so, give them 1 or 2 points of Defense. Attributes: Swords 6 Pentacles 1 Cups 1 Wands 4 Health/Defense: 6/0 Likes: Almost Nothing Hates: Life, Sound, Light

84.title: Notes
84.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature Stats › Skeleton › Notes
84.body: - Breathless and Undreaming . Skeletons ignore any effects related to living processes. They do not breathe. They do not sleep. They cannot be poisoned. They are immune to the Poison Blood of seablooded orcs. - Empty Skulls . Skeletons ignore any attempts to manipulate their minds. They are immune to the Inspire effect. They cannot see illusions. - Fleshless . Skeletons are immune to piercing weapons such as arrows and spears. Actions that target skeletons must exceed (not just match) their Initiative.

85.title: Lesser dooms
85.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature Stats › Skeleton › Lesser dooms
85.body: - Unearthly Fear . Play a lesser doom card and compare its value to the Initiative of each character in the same zone. If the skeleton does this on its turn, it adds its Wands to the total value. Adventurers it succeeds against are Stunned.

86.title: Greater dooms
86.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature Stats › Skeleton › Greater dooms
86.body: - Absorb Bones . If there is a ready source of bones in the skeleton’s zone (e.g., a defeated skeleton), play a greater doom to take those bones. This Heals the skeleton.

87.title: Theme and Threat
87.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature Stats › Theme and Threat
87.body: Health/Defense (HD) Health is a creature’s general toughness, defense is their armor; see Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase. For example, a creature with HD 6/0 has 6 Health and 0 Defense. Notes Everything special the GM needs to remember to run the creature is listed here. Often, notes list invulnerabilities or abilities that do not require an action to invoke. Lesser dooms During a Challenge, lesser dooms are activated by playing major arcana cards with values of 1-14; see Lesser dooms. Attributes Just like adventurers, creatures have attributes. Add them to their action values when they take their turns during a Challenge. Likes and Hates Engaging with things the creature likes prompts positive Dispositions. Antagonize the creature with things it hates to create negative Dispositions. See see Social Encounters & Disposition. Greater dooms During a Challenge, greater dooms are activated by playing major arcana cards with values of 15-21; see Greater dooms. Theme defines the story of the creature. Threat defines how dangerous the creature is.

88.title: Creature actions
88.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature actions
88.body: Rules for the sample dungeon denizens refer to different types of actions. It’s our hope that natural language guides your interpretations during play instead of a relentless pursuit of a pure text legalism. To this end, here’s some insight into the words we’ve chosen to describe the actions on the following pages.

89.title: Free actions
89.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature actions › Free actions
89.body: Free actions can be performed without playing a card . This might be once a turn (e.g., a creature can Move once each turn without the GM playing a card) or when certain conditions are met (e.g., if a creature is the target of a spell, they can Heal 1 Wound as a free action).

90.title: Standard Challenge Actions
90.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature actions › Standard Challenge Actions
90.body: The GM uses the same list of Challenge Actions as the players do. Creatures use standard Challenge Actions by playing a lesser doom card. Sometimes, however, creatures might have special rules for standard Challenge Actions. For example, a creature might deal 2 Wounds with an Attack action or move 3 zones instead of 2 with a Dash action. As a reminder, the creature adds the action’s associated attribute to the action’s total value on their turn. When making a minor action, the creature can play any lesser doom card but does not add their attribute.

91.title: Miscellaneous actions
91.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature actions › Miscellaneous actions
91.body: Miscellaneous actions are actions where the card’s value doesn’t matter (Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit)). A creature can play either a lesser doom or greater doom card to make a miscellaneous action.

92.title: “Play a card”
92.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature actions › “Play a card”
92.body: When the GM uses a card from their hand to activate an ability or perform an action that takes some amount of time, we call it “playing a card.” Creatures can usually only play one card per turn, like adventurers. The text will specify if a particular type of card needs to be played (lesser doom vs greater doom, even value vs odd value, etc.).

93.title: “Discard a card”
93.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature actions › “Discard a card”
93.body: When the GM needs to use a card to activate an ability that requires an incidental amount of time or effort, we call it “discarding a card.” There are no limits to the amount of cards the GM can discard per round (except, of course, how many cards they have in their hand). The text will specify if a particular type of card needs to be discarded (lesser doom vs greater doom, even value vs odd value, etc.).

94.title: “As an Attack”
94.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Monstrous Mixology › Creature actions › “As an Attack”
94.body: Some creatures’ abilities modify Attack actions. For example, a creature might target two separate adventurers with each Attack action or deal an effect in addition to a Wound. If a creature has multiple dooms that activate when they Attack, the GM chooses only one per Attack action. Often, greater doom abilities are activated when the creature discards a greater doom card while making an Attack. The Attack action is used by playing a lesser doom card, comparing the action’s total value against the target’s Initiative as normal. At the same time, the creature discards any greater doom card to activate the special ability. If the Attack hits, the target takes an additional effect. If the Attack misses, the greater doom card is wasted.

96.title: Beast
96.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Beast
96.body: Creatures from the realm of Flesh are “natural” creatures. This includes animals that exist in the real world (bears, snakes, wolves) and those who appear only in medieval bestiaries (cockatrices and krakens). There’s an enormous amount of inspiration to be found in medieval understandings of animals. According to medieval bestiaries, panthers have a sweet-smelling breath that lures dragons, pelicans feed their young with their own blood, and goat’s blood can melt diamonds. Subvert tropes by making these myths real for your game.

97.title: Beast template
97.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Beast › Beast template
97.body: Likes: Its Mate, Its Young, Easy Sources of Food Hates: Fire

98.title: Notes
98.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Beast › Beast template › Notes
98.body: - Fleet . On its turn , the beast can Move 1 zone without spending a card.

99.title: Lesser dooms
99.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Beast › Beast template › Lesser dooms
99.body: (Choose 1 of the following) - Bite . On a successful Attack, the target is also either Disarmed or Tripped (GM’s choice). - Claw . On a successful Attack, if the beast’s total Attack value is double the Initiative of the target , deal 2 Wounds. - Special Locomotion . The beast has a special type of movement—flight, burrowing, climbing, etc. The beast can Move in this way to avoid the adventurers and leave the area (unless the adventurers have some way to keep up). - Trample . On an unsuccessful Attack , the beast may use their Attack action against a second target in the same zone.

100.title: Elemental
100.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Elemental
100.body: Elementals are defined by the habitat in which they live. They are the inhabitants, guardians, or personification of natural phenomena. Elementals are cousins to spirits even though they’re native to the realm of Flesh. They understand the practicalities of temporal experience more completely than those from the far realms. Still, they are not the same as elves, orcs, and humans—they are strangers, coming in contact with mortals only rarely. Elementals can be at turns helpful and harmful, capricious and caring. This group includes humanoid, intelligent creatures (mermaids, dryads), animal-like creatures (salamanders, thunderbirds), and creatures composed of animated elemental energy (tree giants, fire elementals).

101.title: Elemental template
101.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Elemental › Elemental template
101.body: Likes: Learning About Mortals Hates: Elemental Opposition (Fire vs Water, Air vs Earth), Trespassing

102.title: Notes
102.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Elemental › Elemental template › Notes
102.body: - Elemental Immunity . An elemental takes no damage from their chosen element. A huldra cannot drown. A salamander cannot be burned. A tree giant shrugs off weapons made of wood. - Elemental Travel . In their natural environment , the elemental can Move 1 zone without spending a card each turn.

103.title: Lesser dooms
103.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Elemental › Elemental template › Lesser dooms
103.body: - Engulf . The elemental can attempt to pull an adventurer into their element as a Roughhouse action: air elementals pull the adventurer into the air and drop them, water elementals pull them under the water, etc. This deals Piercing damage.

104.title: Man
104.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Man
104.body: “Man” is a misnomer; the term is chosen merely because it sounds archaic. This theme includes the sentient people (humans, elves, gnomes, etc.). These are people, not Underworld creatures.

105.title: Man template
105.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Man › Man template
105.body: There isn’t one, really. Represent people in your game by making actual characters. If the character is strange or monstrous (like a mutant or a ghoulish cannibal), give them a few special greater dooms that represent their core gimmick.

106.title: Sorcerous
106.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Sorcerous
106.body: There are blasphemies summoned into this world by sorcerers playing god. Sorcerers are full of bad ideas. “What if I created a bear with the head of an owl? What if I made this albino ape sentient? What if I made one really big eye float around?” Awful. Nobody likes sorcerers. Sorcerous creatures include all manner of abominations, experiments, maleficence side effects, and cursed entities.

107.title: Sorcerous template
107.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Sorcerous › Sorcerous template
107.body: Likes: Magic, Eating Strange Things (Brains, Coins, Curses), Radioactive Materials Hates: Beauty, Music, Children’s Laughter

108.title: Notes
108.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Sorcerous › Sorcerous template › Notes
108.body: - Smell Magic . The creature can smell magical effects. They can identify who is and isn’t a sorcerer by scent. - Strange Body . (Optional) Many sorcerous creatures are invulnerable to a certain type of harm (fire, weapons, acid, blunt force trauma, etc.). At the same time, they are explicitly vulnerable from another common type of harm and take 2 Wounds instead of 1 from this source (electricity, cold temperatures, poison, etc.). Sorcerous creatures do not have any default lesser dooms.

109.title: Spirit
109.breadcrumb: Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens › Themes › Spirit
109.body: There are dream worlds called the far realms outside of this reality. The beings that dwell in those places do not have physical forms, but must clothe themselves in flesh when visiting this realm. These creatures are called spirits because they are not naturally physical. The four far realms are the Waste, Weald, Weird, and Welkin. They are described (imperfectly) in Appendix A, see The Weird. It is said devils live in the Waste. It is said that daemons live in the Weald. It is said that jinni live in the Weird. It is said that angels live in the Welkin. These spirits are alien creatures with an alien understanding of the realm of Flesh. They are baffled by the ideas of food, evolution, skin, isolated sensory experiences, and other mundane events.
